profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Salt Lake City - Millcreek) is located at 3949 South 200 East, Suite B1, Salt Lake City, UT 84107. The operator publishes a footprint of 36000 square feet and 1.92 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18, HIPAA. This building is one of six Flexential locations serving the Salt Lake City market. Salt Lake City's data center sector is drawn in part by some of the lowest electricity and natural gas rates in the nation, historically around 5 to 6 cents per kilowatt-hour from a mix of natural gas and renewable generation, a cooling-efficient high-desert climate, and Utah's sales-and-use tax exemption for data center equipment purchases at facilities exceeding 150,000 square feet, retroactive to mid-2016, according to industry market analysis. Seismic activity along the Wasatch Front is a real engineering consideration for the region's data centers, mitigated through structural design. Other major operators active in the broader Salt Lake City market include DataBank in Bluffdale, Aligned Data Centers in West Jordan, Novva Data Centers, QTS in Eagle Mountain, Meta, and Oracle, reflecting the area's shift from smaller retail colocation toward larger enterprise, HPC, and hyperscale capacity.

Flexential itself traces to the 1999 founding of ViaWest, which built out a Western US colocation footprint including Utah before merging with the Southeast-focused Peak 10 in 2017 and rebranding as Flexential in 2018; the company is now privately held with GI Partners as controlling sponsor. Utah's data center water use has drawn growing state scrutiny: a bill from Rep. Jill Koford, advanced unanimously by a legislative water panel in November 2025 for the 2026 session, would require data centers to report annual water consumption to the state under a $10,000-per-day fine for non-compliance, with individual figures kept anonymized publicly but available to state water officials. Reporting on the bill cited examples ranging from facilities using up to 5 million gallons a day, more than 12,000 times a typical household's usage, to the NSA's Bluffdale, Utah facility at about 23 million gallons annually, against low-water designs like Novva's reported 85,000 gallons; Koford said state water regulators had previously been left out of data-center water-use oversight, which had been handled mainly through city permitting.

reading.body:
Flexential Salt Lake City - Millcreek publishes 1.92 MW of critical load UPS capacity across 36,000 square feet, representing 3.7 percent of Utah's documented 52.18 MW total. At typical AI training density this accommodates roughly 48 racks, too small for large-scale model work.

The facility holds security certifications including NIST 800-53, ITAR, and SOC 2 Type II, positioning it for sensitive enterprise colocation, backup systems, and compliance-heavy workloads in defense, finance, and healthcare rather than dense compute clusters. Its design reflects purpose rather than scale.

Utah's constraint for AI infrastructure assessment is not this facility but the opacity of most of the state's mapped sites. Of 21 facilities on record, the majority do not publish capacity figures. The state's total revealed capacity of 52.18 MW ranks it far below regions built for compute density, and the missing data makes even that total incomplete as a measure of actual available power.
